common_name: Stuart Boothman Bleeding Heart (Compact Rose-Pink Fernleaf Dicentra)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in early spring into moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; spreads gently by rhizome to form a tidy low colony over a few seasons.

directions: Stuart Boothman is a UK-raised selection prized for its exceptionally fine, silvery blue-gray, deeply dissected foliage and abundant sprays of nodding, deep rose-pink heart-shaped flowers held just above the leaves from mid-spring into early summer. It is noticeably more compact and floriferous than the wild Pacific bleeding heart, making it well suited to the front of a shaded border or a woodland path edge where its foliage color can be appreciated up close alongside hostas and ferns. Provide consistently moist, humus-rich soil and cool root conditions; the plant may thin out or pause in hot, dry summer spells but rebounds with cooler, moister weather and returns reliably each spring. Divide congested clumps in early spring to rejuvenate plantings or increase stock.

This naturally occurring pink-flowered form of bloodroot was found in the wild and is maintained by specialty native-plant growers for gardeners who want a soft blush of color rather than the species' typical pure white; unlike the fully double 'Multiplex', it keeps the single, eight-to-ten-petaled bloodroot flower form but in a pale to medium pink. Plant rhizome divisions shallowly, just below the soil surface, in humus-rich, evenly moist, slightly acidic woodland soil beneath deciduous trees, where the emerging leaf wraps protectively around the flower bud before unfurling. Like the species, it is a true spring ephemeral that flowers before the tree canopy leafs out and then goes completely dormant by early summer, so mark its location and interplant with later-emerging ferns or hostas to fill the gap. Handle rhizomes with care, as the orange-red sap can stain skin and fabric.
